contexts.context: Globally Lipschitz mapping between metric spaces

formulations.label: global-two-point-condition
formulations.text: Let (X,d_X) and (Y,d_Y) be metric spaces and f:X→Y. The map f is globally Lipschitz on X if there exists L≥0 such that d_Y(f(x),f(y))≤L d_X(x,y) for every x,y∈X.

contexts.context: Source-specific anchored Lipschitz bound at a selected point, not necessarily locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood

formulations.label: anchored-at-point-condition
formulations.text: For a∈X and f:(X,d_X)→(Y,d_Y), the source's Lipschitz-at-a condition is the existence of L≥0 such that d_Y(f(x),f(a))≤L d_X(x,a) for every x∈X; only one input is fixed at a.

mathematical_review: The source independently states both the global two-variable Lipschitz condition and a point-anchored (one fixed argument) condition. Global Lipschitz implies the anchored bound for every point, but an anchored bound at one point does not imply a uniform two-point Lipschitz constant on any neighborhood. It should not be conflated with the common 'locally Lipschitz at a' convention requiring the two-point inequality on some neighborhood of a. ProofWiki also gives a real-interval specialization; here that is documented as a specialization, not counted as an additional independent context. No requirement that X be complete, compact or connected.

contexts.context: Unrooted simple connected acyclic graph, with no finiteness assumption

formulations.label: no-circuits
formulations.text: An (unrooted) tree is a simple connected graph that contains no circuits (nontrivial closed edge-trails).

formulations.label: no-cycles
formulations.text: Equivalently, an (unrooted) tree is a simple connected graph containing no cycles.

mathematical_review: ProofWiki supplies two equivalent presentations of unrooted simple connected acyclic graphs: no circuits and no cycles. For undirected simple graphs, a circuit contains a cycle, making their absence equivalent, even without finiteness; they should share one mathematical meaning with two individually sourced formulations. The source separately mentions rooted tree as an alternative terminology, but the root, parent and child structures are not independently defined here; do not silently turn the unrooted meaning into a rooted tree. A tree can be finite or infinite; do not impose finite vertex set. The empty-graph connectedness convention is not settled by this source and must not be asserted.

contexts.context: Two P-independent sub-sigma-algebras of one probability space

formulations.label: binary-event-factorization
formulations.text: For a probability space (Ω,F,P) and sub-σ-algebras G₁,G₂⊆F, the pair is independent if P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) for every A∈G₁ and B∈G₂.

contexts.context: Countably indexed family of mutually P-independent sub-sigma-algebras

formulations.label: all-finite-distinct-index-factorization
formulations.text: For (Ω,F,P) and a sequence (G_n) of sub-σ-algebras of F, the sequence is mutually independent if for every finite set of distinct indices i₁,…,i_m (m≥1) and every A_j∈G_{i_j}, P(⋂_{j=1}^m A_j)=∏_{j=1}^m P(A_j).

mathematical_review: Both source sections are independently visible and their quantifiers differ: binary independence is the event-product criterion for two sub-σ-algebras, whereas an indexed family requires factorization for all finite collections of DISTINCT indices. Mere pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence for three or more σ-algebras, so these are separate mathematical contexts rather than equivalent presentations of one fixed family property. The countable formulation does not require countable intersections of arbitrary events in the condition; only finite subsets are tested. All events must be measurable in the same ambient probability space. This source has an incidental inconsistent notation for the ambient σ-algebra in its binary paragraph, resolved by the explicit surrounding probability-space notation rather than quoted verbatim.

contexts.context: Countable family of measurable-space-valued independent random variables

formulations.label: generated-sigma-algebra-mutual-independence
formulations.text: Let (Ω,F,P) be a probability space, (S,Σ_S) a measurable target space, and X_n:Ω→S measurable for each n. The sequence (X_n) is mutually independent if the σ-algebras σ(X_n)={X_n⁻¹(B):B∈Σ_S} form a mutually independent sequence of sub-σ-algebras of F.

mathematical_review: ProofWiki defines a sequence of random variables taking values in one measurable space as independent precisely when their generated σ-algebras are mutually independent. The generated σ-algebra is X_n^{-1}(S), i.e. the collection of preimages of all measurable subsets of S, not the single preimage of the whole target S. The notation (S,Σ_S) explicitly distinguishes the target underlying set and its σ-algebra, and the generated σ-algebra formula quantifies over all B∈Σ_S. This is joint/mutual independence of all finite distinct subcollections, NOT merely pairwise independence, and does not require that the X_n are real-valued. Its prerequisites can be checked against independently screened random-variable, probability-space and independent-σ-algebra meanings after source intake.
